So what are, what are, what attracts these congressmen?
You know, HDI, they market themselves as a, as a global middleman, as a global power broker.
And they set up acquaintances, they set up meetings, they do facilitate trips all over the world.
They, so when they, when they come in and they, they set up their congressional advisory board, they suddenly link this congressman up with interests all over the globe.
Whether they be business interests, whether they be political interests, whether they be any other form of Intel interest.

They are, they definitely appear to have some very strange Intel ties.

And they, that's what they openly cast themselves as doing.
They, they set it up and they let it play out.
They're used as a vessel sort of for their CCP tie.
This story is, I think, a bombshell in the sense that we should be internalizing it as the equivalent of the World Health Organization and their pandemic treaty.
This is kind of the United Nations approach to misinformation in that context.
In other words, they want to take away sovereignty from the United States, from our government and put it to kind of the level above, right?
Extract one level up and have really the United Nations be able to determine what exactly constitutes misinformation.

Now I know that's a mouthful, but if you really drill down and you read the document or at least the draft document,
it really has to do with people who share information that the UN would deem misinformation.
In some cases, it's people who promote ideological hatred or political hatred.
People who also promote, they say, terrorism or trying to overthrow the government.
But as we've seen, those terms are often misappropriated and right weaponized against people who dare to defy the globalist kind of world order.
And I think the key point to focus on here, which we'll get into later, but is how China is actually trying to shape this treaty, this convention.
And they've actually put forth a resolution to be added to this document.
And I'll read it briefly because it really is scary.

And they say they want to criminalize people who share false information that could result in serious social disorder, including but not limited to information related to natural and human caused disasters.
In other words, to me, that means they're talking about a lab leak and a potentially future pandemic or artificially create a natural disaster.
But that is right out of the CCP's mouth, this concept of social disorder.
That's how kind of the new term that they're going to be using to silence us.

And it's really scary that the UN is actually partnering not just with member states like China, but also private companies, including Meta, the American Chamber of Commerce, Amazon Web Services and Microsoft.
They're part of the ad hoc committee advising the UN on the formulation of this committee.
So this is a really big story that that is worth paying attention to.
It's up on war room.org if you want to read it.
What is the timing of all this?
When's this convention?
Just walk me through a critical path here.
Sure.
So the effort to roll this out began in December 2019.
That was when the UN voted to kind of get the groundwork going to establish this convention and it'll be formalized.
So the document what I'm speaking about now is a draft, but it'll be totally done.
The deliberative process completed in September of 2024.
So they're really taking their time.

so-called manmade or natural human disasters to sort of broaden their purview over what they can and can't censor.
In addition to some states in the U.S. that banned TikTok, the EU is more closely scrutinizing the platform.
Recently, the Dutch Ministry of General Affairs asked ministries and government agencies to stop using the Chinese application TikTok.

Two Dutch government officials told Politico that Dutch government ministries and agencies have mostly followed the requirement of the general department to avoid using TikTok and that the government has stopped communicating and advertising on this platform.
This is despite the app's skyrocketing popularity in the Netherlands, which has around 3.5 million users.

The decision to ban TikTok came after the announcement by the Dutch Ministry of General Affairs last November that the government suspends the use of TikTok until this app adjusts its data protection policy.
While the proposal is similar to the U.S. government's decision to ban TikTok on their devices starting in December, the Dutch ban is more limited in range and enforcement, according to Politico.

According to Taiwan's Newtons newspaper, the general department is an executive body headed by the prime minister of the Netherlands tasked with coordinating government policy, communicating with the royal family, and more.

The office of the prime minister, the Dutch government press service, the government science and policy committee, and the intelligence and security oversight committee are all managed by the general department.
TikTok, owned by ByteDance, a Chinese multinational internet technology company, has been investigated for sending EU user data to China.
More than half of U.S. states have banned TikTok's access to the app on state government devices.
The U.S. federal government and Congress also banned it.

French President Emmanuel Macron, one of Europe's fiercest critics of TikTok, described TikTok as seemingly innocent but is a cause of making users addicted and a source of misinformation from Russia.
On January 12, France fined TikTok $5.5 million for errors in handling cookies.
On July 2021, the Dutch Data Protection Authority issued a fine of $800,000 against TikTok for invading the privacy of young children.

The reason is that TikTok does not fully display the terms of privacy and data protection in Dutch, while many teenagers, mostly young children, cannot know how their data will be processed because they don't learn English.

Politico reported Dutch officials have sought to strengthen ties with Washington in recent months as the United States pushed to limit sales of sensitive technology to China, including machinery made by a Dutch ASML company.
Dutch Prime Minister Mark Rutte met with President Joe Biden this month and discussed countermeasures to China's threat.
TikTok admitted in early November last year that some Chinese employees had access to TikTok user data in Europe.
In December, a Forbes report said that TikTok employees used a way to access user data to track reporters' locations, so it was strictly investigated in the U.S.
On January 10, the head of the EU's antitrust department, Margarethe Vestegar, asked TikTok CEO Joe Zizi to meet in Brussels, Belgium, to jointly reevaluate EU-China relations more broadly.
TikTok is facing numerous legal, regulatory, and security challenges in the EU and growing criticism from the public.

On January 19, after a video call with Zhou Zizi, EU internal market commissioner Thierry Breton said that if the audit results show that TikTok is not fully compliant with the EU Digital Service Act, we will not hesitate to implement comprehensive sanctions to protect our citizens.
